newsitem.title: USA: U.S. says both sides responsible in Hebron talks.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says both sides responsible in Hebron talks.

text.p: The United States said on Monday that the Palestinians alone could not be blamed for the failure so far to reach an agreement on an Israeli pull-back in Hebron, and it remained confident a deal would be reached.

Dismissing suggestions that the talks had collapsed, State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said U.S. envoy Dennis Ross, who was returning to Washington on Monday, was likely to go back to the Middle East in some days to resume mediation.

Some Israeli officials suggested Palestinian President Yasser Arafat was stalling the talks by embarking on Monday on a European tour. Israel's ambassador to Washington said Arafat had rejected a plea by Ross to call off the trip.
Burns would not confirm that Ross had made such a request.

But he said: "I think it's wrong, and I think it's also just not consistent with the facts to point at Chairman Arafat and say: 'He's the guy holding these talks up' or 'Had he stayed these talks would have succeeded today or tomorrow'."

"I would just look at both of them (Israelis and Palestinians) and say they're both responsible, and they're only going to get an agreement when both of them cross the line together," he told a news briefing.

The departure of Arafat and Ross followed a major U.S. push to clinch an agreement on the key issue of the West Bank town of Hebron, with President Bill Clinton telephoning Arafat and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Sunday.
Officials say the talks are to continue at a lower level until the Palestinian leader returns from his European tour, which began with a visit to Norway.

Burns sought to paint a hopeful scenario, saying: "Our expectation of an agreement has been confirmed by the results of the last three weeks, particularly ... the last week, where a significant amount of progress was made."

"At some point, I would think shortly, Dennis will be going back to the region," he added. "We believe -- collectively and individually -- that this agreement's going to be made, and we're not panicking."

The U.S. spokesman's assessment differed sharply from that offered earlier by Israeli ambassador Eliahu Ben Elissar, who said Israel had expected to wrap up the deal early on Monday only to find that the Palestinians had "reopened" several issues.

Burns said he was not aware that either side had sought to reopen agreed issues in the last 24 hours. "I don't think anyone's hardening their position," he said, adding that he believed agreement was "very close".

According to Israeli and Palestinian officials, the main sticking points are Israel's right of "hot pursuit" into PLO-controlled areas of Hebron, following any guerrilla attack, and the type of arms to be used by Palestinian police.

Israel was supposed to redeploy last spring in Hebron, where some 450 Jews live among more than 100,000 Arabs, but the move was postponed after guerrilla truck bombings in Israel. Israel has redeployed in six other West Bank towns.

Burns agreed with Ben Elissar on one point, that there would be little point in the Palestinians waiting until after the Nov. 5 U.S. presidential elections -- as some Israeli officials say they are -- in hope of winning a better deal.
"We don't want to encourage anyone to think that the day following an election, should President Clinton be victorious, American foreign policy is going to fundamentally change," Burns said.
